dialogs.title: Dialogue — En aftale i kalenderen
dialogs.intro: Budi and Mette find a time to study together.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Skal vi læse sammen i denne uge?
lines.id: Shall we study together this week?
lines.literal: shall we read together in this week?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Onsdag kan jeg ikke. Jeg har time til fire.
lines.id: I can't on Wednesday. I have class until four.
lines.literal: Wednesday can I not. I have lesson till four.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvad med torsdag? Kvart over fem?
lines.id: What about Thursday? A quarter past five?
lines.literal: what with Thursday? quarter over five?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det passer fint. Hvor mødes vi?
lines.id: That works fine. Where shall we meet?
lines.literal: it suits fine. where meet we?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: På biblioteket. Det åbner klokken otte og lukker klokken syv.
lines.id: At the library. It opens at eight and closes at seven.
lines.literal: on library-the. it opens clock-the eight and closes clock-the seven.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Perfekt. Men jeg kommer måske lidt for sent.
lines.id: Perfect. But I might be a little late.
lines.literal: perfect. but I come maybe little too late.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Halv seks, måske. Bussen er aldrig til tiden.
lines.id: Half past five, maybe. The bus is never on time.
lines.literal: half six, maybe. bus-the is never to time-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det er i orden. Vi ses på torsdag!
lines.id: That's fine. See you on Thursday!
lines.literal: it is in order. we see-each-other on Thursday!

notes: **Halv seks = 5:30, not 6:30.** Danish counts the half toward the next hour — *halv seks* means "half (way to) six". This is a nasty trap for English speakers: in British English *half six* means 6:30, so a Dane's *halv seks* is a whole hour earlier than you'd think.
**Klokken** = "the clock", from *en klokke* (bell, clock) with the definite ending. In writing it's often shortened to *kl.*, and in fast speech it almost disappears.

**Passer** from *at passe* = to suit, to fit. *Det passer fint* = that suits me fine. The word also means "to look after" (*at passe børn* = to look after children) and "to be true" (*det passer ikke* = that's not true).
**Jeg har time** — *en time* means two things: an hour, and a lesson. *Jeg har time til fire* = I have class until four. (Not English "time" — that's *tid*.)
**For sent** = late. Remember *for* means "too", so literally "too late". Being on time in Denmark isn't extra politeness, it's the default — an appointment at two means two, not ten past.

**Mødes** — a form ending in *-s* that means "each other": *at møde* (to meet someone) → *at mødes* (to meet each other). The same pattern is in *vi ses* (we see each other = see you) and *vi snakkes ved* (we'll talk later).
**Aldrig** = never. Note there's no *ikke* in that sentence — *aldrig* already contains the negation, just like English *never*.
**På torsdag** = this coming Thursday. Without *på*, *torsdag* just means Thursday in general. And *om torsdagen* means "every Thursday, on Thursdays".

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: In conversation Danish uses the twelve-hour clock, with four reference points each hour: on the hour, quarter past, half, and quarter to.
after: ⚠️ The 5:25 and 5:35 rows are the trickiest. In that range Danish doesn't count from the full hour but from the **half**: *fem minutter i halv seks* (five minutes before half to six) and *fem minutter over halv seks*. German and Dutch do the same.
Official schedules — trains, buses, cinemas, opening hours — use the 24-hour clock and are read straight: *sytten tredive* for 17:30. Don't mix the two.
To ask: *Hvad er klokken?* (what time is it?) and *Hvornår…?* (when…?). To say at what time something happens, use *klokken* with no preposition: *Toget kommer klokken ni.*

grammars.title: Days, months, parts of the day
body: All of them are written in **lowercase** — unlike English. The day names come from Norse gods, just like English *Wednesday*, *Thursday* and *Friday*.
after: *Onsdag* = Odin's day (English *Wednesday*, from Woden), *torsdag* = Thor's day, *fredag* = Freya's day. *Lørdag*, though, means "washing day" (*løre* = to wash) — a Viking habit of bathing once a week, and the name has survived a thousand years.

Parts of the day: *om morgenen* (in the morning), *om formiddagen* (late morning), *om eftermiddagen* (afternoon), *om aftenen* (evening), *om natten* (at night). Note they all use **om** + the form with the ending.
⚠️ Three ways of using a day name, each with a different meaning: *på mandag* (next Monday), *om mandagen* (every Monday), *i mandags* (last Monday).

blocks.text: *Desværre* = unfortunately. It softens a refusal and almost always comes along when you turn down an invitation. Without it, *det kan jeg ikke* sounds flat and a bit cold.

blocks.title: Time in Denmark isn't an estimate
items: An appointment at two means two. Turning up at ten past without letting anyone know is considered rude, not relaxed.
If you're going to be late, send a message. Ready-made sentence: *Jeg kommer ti minutter for sent — undskyld!*
On the other hand, don't arrive too early at someone's home. Turning up fifteen minutes early actually bothers a host who isn't ready yet.

blocks.text: The phrase *i orden* (literally "in order") means "fine, no problem". It's used very often as a casual reply: *Det er i orden.*
*Et øjeblik* literally means "an eye-blink" — a direct cousin of German *Augenblick*. Used on its own it means "just a moment": *Et øjeblik!*
